claims.claim: Investing is putting money into assets such as stocks or bonds with the expectation of making a return over time; this is the working definition used in the lesson, attributed to SEC Investor.gov.
A return from an investment may come from an increase in the asset's value or from the asset's interest or dividend payments to its owners.

Saving and investing both mean setting aside money, but they differ: savings accounts suit short-term goals and emergency funds with stable, typically insured money, while investing puts money into assets whose value can fluctuate in pursuit of growth; the U.S. government's MyMoney.gov groups both under one SAVE & INVEST pillar.
All investments involve some degree of risk; risk is the degree of uncertainty and/or potential financial loss inherent in an investment decision.

Market fluctuations are normal: large-company stocks as a group have lost money on average about one out of every three years, and prices can move up or down even when companies are not in danger of failing.

A time horizon is the number of months, years, or decades an investor needs to hold money to achieve a financial goal; money for long-term goals can allow for market fluctuations over time, while money needed in the near future favors options with less potential risk and volatility.

The main investment choices include stocks (a type of security giving a share of ownership in a company), bonds (debt securities similar to IOUs issued by borrowers), and funds (companies that pool money from many investors into a portfolio of securities, such as mutual funds and ETFs).

Diversification spreads money among many different investments so that if one loses money the others may make up for those losses — 'don't put all your eggs in one basket'; it reduces the impact of any single loss without promising gains.

The general practice of investing is regular investing — putting a set dollar amount or a set percentage of income into investment accounts on a schedule; starting earlier makes compounding more powerful while starting later means needing to invest more, so small regular amounts over time beat waiting for a perfect moment.
Investing has no set rate of return and all investments carry risk, so the honest framing is that investing is a long game with real risk rather than a guaranteed path to gains.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether investing can be described as having a typical or expected return
positions: Investor.gov notes that some experts consider a 7–10% annual rate of return a useful estimate for long-term diversified investments in U.S. stocks, based on historic averages.
The same page stresses that investing does not have a set rate of return and that all investments involve risk, with fluctuations to be expected over time.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson quotes no return figure and promises no returns; it presents the honest framing (long game, real risk, no set rate of return) and leaves return math to the finance subject.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether saving and investing are one activity or two
positions: Investor.gov treats them as related but distinct: savings accounts for short-term goals and emergency funds, investing for growth in assets whose value fluctuates.
MyMoney.gov groups both under a single pillar, SAVE & INVEST, as building blocks for managing and growing money.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps them distinct on the risk axis (stability vs growth with risk), notes the shared family under MyMoney's pillar, and points to the saving sibling topic for depth.

positions: Investor.gov's glossary frames diversification as spreading money among various investments in the hope that if one loses money the others make up for those losses.
Marketing language sometimes implies that a diversified fund is effectively safe.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that diversification reduces the impact of a single loss but does not promise gains, and that all investments still involve risk.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Investing
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition of investing (putting money into assets such as stocks or bonds with the expectation of making a return over time); return as an increase in the asset's value or interest/dividend payments; saving vs investing framing (savings accounts for short-term goals and emergency funds); all investments involve risk and investors should allow for market fluctuations over time; time horizon (long-term = decades; money needed soon favors lower-risk options); regular investing as a set dollar amount or percentage of income; starting earlier makes compounding more powerful and starting later means investing more; no set rate of return. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. sourceRecords.title: Diversification (Investor.gov glossary)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator glossary). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: diversification as the strategy summed up as 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' — spreading money among various investments in the hope that if one loses money the others make up for those losses. The 'hope' framing supports the lesson's honest note that diversification reduces risk without promising gains.

sourceRecords.title: Asset Allocation and Diversification (Investor.gov, Getting Started)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: diversification as the practice of spreading money among different investments to reduce risk; allocating among different kinds of assets because conditions that hurt one asset class may improve another; spreading within each asset class across many stocks or bonds and across industry sectors. The lesson uses it for the personal version of diversification across companies, industries, and asset types.
